canonical.:question/problem:
Find the general solution to the differential equation

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}y} {\textrm{d}x} + \dfrac{y}{x}  = \dfrac{x^2}{y} .
$$
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that our equation is an instance of the Bernoulli differential equation

$$
\dfrac{{{\rm{d}}y}}{{{\rm{d}}x}} + p(x)y= q(x)y^n.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
p(x) = \dfrac{1}{x}, \qquad q(x) = x^2, \qquad n=-1.
$$

First, we divide the differential equation by $y^{-1},$ and we get

$$
y \dfrac{{{\rm{d}}y}}{{{\rm{d}}x}} + \dfrac{y^{2}}{x}= x^2.
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z= y^{1-n} =  y^{2}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x}  = 2y \,\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
y\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{1}{2}\,\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x}.
$$

 

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z(x)$ as follows:

$$
\dfrac{1}{2}\,\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x} + \dfrac{1}{x}z  = x^2
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. But first, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x} + \dfrac{2}{x} z
		=2x^2
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x} + P(x)z = Q(x)
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=\frac{2}{x},\,Q(x)=2{x}^{2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (2/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & ={x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)=x^2$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{2}{x}z) & ={x}^{2}\cdot (2{x}^{2}) \\ {x}^{2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+2xz & =2{x}^{4} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(z{x}^{2}) & =2{x}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(z{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int 2{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x \\ z{x}^{2} & =\frac{2{x}^{5}}{5}+{C}_{1} \\ z & =\frac{2{x}^{5}+C}{5{x}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=5C_1.$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z=y^{2}.$ This results in the general solution

$$
y^{ 2} =\dfrac{2x^5 + C}{5x^2}.
$$

nearby.:question/problem:
Find the general solution to the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-y={y}^{2}{e}^{x}.
$$
nearby.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that our equation is an instance of the Bernoulli differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+p(x)y=q(x){y}^{n}.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
p(x)=-1,\,q(x)={e}^{x},\,n=2.
$$

First, we divide the differential equation by ${y}^{2},$ and we get

$$
{y}^{-2}\frac{dy}{dx}-{y}^{-1}={e}^{x}.\,\,(∗)
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{1-n}={y}^{-1}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=-{y}^{-2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,{y}^{-2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

 

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z(x)$ as follows:

$$
-\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-z={e}^{x}
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. But first, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+z=-{e}^{x}
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x)
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=1,\,Q(x)=-{e}^{x}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (1)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)={e}^{x}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+z) & ={e}^{x}\cdot (-{e}^{x}) \\ {e}^{x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+z{e}^{x} & =-{e}^{2x} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(z{e}^{x}) & =-{e}^{2x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(z{e}^{x})\,\text{d}x & =-\int {e}^{2x}\,\text{d}x \\ z{e}^{x} & =-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2x}+{C}_{1} \\ z & =\frac{C-{e}^{2x}}{2{e}^{x}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=2{C}_{1}.$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z={y}^{-1}.$ This results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{-1}=\frac{C-{e}^{2x}}{2{e}^{x}}\,⇒\,y=\frac{2{e}^{x}}{C-{e}^{2x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

q.:question/problem:
Consider the inexact differential equation
$x^{2}ydx - (x^{3} + 2y^{4})dy = 0$.
It is known that
$$
\displaystyle \frac{1}{P}(\frac{∂P}{∂y} - \frac{∂Q}{∂x}) = \frac{4}{y}
$$
where the functions $P$ and $Q$ are given by
$$
\displaystyle P(x, y) = x^{2}y, Q(x, y) =-x^{3} - 2y^{4}.
$$

Use this information to find a suitable integrating factor $I(y)$ and hence find the general solution to the equation.

A suitable integrating factor is $I(y) =$ {{field-1}}.

The general solution is {{field-2}}, where $c$ is a constant.

title: Solving Inexact Differential Equations Using Integrating Factors

canonical.:question/problem:
Consider the inexact differential equation

$$
\left(x + y^2\right)\,\textrm{d}x + \left(xy + \frac{2}{x}\right)\,\textrm{d}y = 0.
$$

It is known that

$$
\dfrac{1}{Q}\left(\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y}-\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x}\right)=\frac{1}{x}
$$

where the functions $P$ and $Q$ are given by

$$
P(x,y)=x+y^2,\qquad Q(x,y)=xy+\frac{2}{x}.
$$

Use this information to find a suitable integrating factor $I(x)$ and hence find the general solution to the equation.
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
For a differential equation of the form

$$
P(x,y)\,\textrm{d}x+Q(x,y)\,\textrm{d}y=0,
$$

we have that if

$$
\dfrac{1}{Q}\left(\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y}-\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x}\right)=g(x)
$$

where $g(x)$ is independent of $y,$ then an integrating factor for the equation is

$$
I(x)=\exp\left(\int g(x)\,\textrm{d}x\right)
$$

where $\exp(x)$ denotes the exponential function $e^x.$

We are given that

$$
\dfrac{1}{Q}\left(\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y}-\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x}\right)=\frac{1}{x}.
$$

Since $\dfrac{1}{x}$ is a function of $x$ only, we can conclude that the integrating factor for the equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int {x}^{-1}\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & =x.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying our equation by the integrating factor, we arrive at the following exact differential equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}x[(x+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}x+(xy+\frac{2}{x})\,\text{d}y] & =0 \\ \underbrace{({x}^{2}+x{y}^{2})}_{\overset{~}{P}}\,\text{d}x+\underbrace{({x}^{2}y+2)}_{\overset{~}{Q}}\,\text{d}y & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

For this exact equation, we have

$$
\widetilde{P}(x,y)=x^2+xy^2,\qquad
\widetilde{Q}(x,y)=x^2y+2.
$$

To solve the equation, let's first integrate $\widetilde{P}(x,y)$ with respect to $x.$
The result should include an arbitrary function of $y,$ which we'll call $F(y){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}u(x,y) & =\int \overset{~}{P}(x,y)\,\text{d}x+F(y) \\  & =\int ({x}^{2}+x{y}^{2})\,\text{d}x+F(y) \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+\frac{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}{2}+F(y).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, let's integrate $\widetilde{Q}(x,y)$ with respect to $y.$
The result should include an arbitrary function of $x,$ which we'll call $G(x){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}u(x,y) & =\int \overset{~}{Q}(x,y)\,\text{d}y+G(x) \\  & =\int ({x}^{2}y+2)\,\text{d}y+G(x) \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}{2}+2y+G(x).\end{aligned}
$$

Comparing the two solutions, we must have

$$
F(y)=2y,\qquad G(x)=\frac{x^3}{3}.
$$

Therefore, the general solution $u(x,y)=c$ is

$$
\frac{x^3}{3}+\frac{x^2y^2}{2}+2y=c.
$$

Consider the inexact differential equation

$$
(\frac{6{y}^{2}}{x}+4{y}^{3})\,\text{d}x+(4y+3x{y}^{2}+\frac{1}{{x}^{3}})\,\text{d}y=0.
$$

It is known that 

$$

$$

where the functions $P$ and $Q$ are given by 

$$
P(x,y)=\frac{6{y}^{2}}{x}+4{y}^{3},\,Q(x,y)=4y+3x{y}^{2}+\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}.
$$

Use this information to find a suitable integrating factor $I(x)$ and hence find the general solution to the equation.

$\,$ A suitable integrating factor is $I(x)=$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The general solution is {{field-2}}, where $c$ is a constant.
nearby.:question/worked-solution:
For a differential equation of the form

$$
P(x,y)\,\text{d}x+Q(x,y)\,\text{d}y=0,
$$

we have that if

$$
\frac{1}{Q}(\frac{∂P}{∂y}-\frac{∂Q}{∂x})=g(x)
$$

where $g(x)$ is independent of $y,$ then an integrating factor for the equation is

$$
I(x)=\operatorname{exp}⁡(\int g(x)\,\text{d}x)
$$

where $\operatorname{exp}⁡(x)$ denotes the exponential function ${e}^{x}.$

We are given that 

$$
\frac{1}{Q}(\frac{∂P}{∂y}-\frac{∂Q}{∂x})=\frac{3}{x}.
$$

Since $\frac{3}{x}$ is a function of $x$ only, we can conclude that the integrating factor for the equation is 

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int 3{x}^{-1}\text{ }\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{3\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & ={x}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying our equation by the integrating factor, we arrive at the following exact differential equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}[(\frac{6{y}^{2}}{x}+4{y}^{3})\,\text{d}x+(4y+3x{y}^{2}+\frac{1}{{x}^{3}})\,\text{d}y] & =0 \\ \underbrace{(6{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+4{x}^{3}{y}^{3})}_{\overset{~}{P}}\,\text{d}x+\underbrace{(4{x}^{3}y+3{x}^{4}{y}^{2}+1)}_{\overset{~}{Q}}\,\text{d}y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

For this exact equation, we have

$$
\overset{~}{P}(x,y)=6{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+4{x}^{3}{y}^{3},\,\overset{~}{Q}(x,y)=4{x}^{3}y+3{x}^{4}{y}^{2}+1.
$$

To solve the equation, let's first integrate $\overset{~}{P}(x,y)$ with respect to $x.$
The result should include an arbitrary function of $y,$ which we'll call $F(y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}u(x,y) & =\int \overset{~}{P}(x,y)\,\text{d}x+F(y) \\  & =\int (6{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+4{x}^{3}{y}^{3})\,\text{d}x+F(y) \\  & =2{x}^{3}{y}^{2}+{x}^{4}{y}^{3}+F(y).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, let's integrate $\overset{~}{Q}(x,y)$ with respect to $y.$
The result should include an arbitrary function of $x,$ which we'll call $G(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}u(x,y) & =\int \overset{~}{Q}(x,y)\,\text{d}y+G(x) \\  & =\int (4{x}^{3}y+3{x}^{4}{y}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}y+G(x) \\  & =2{x}^{3}{y}^{2}+{x}^{4}{y}^{3}+y+G(x).\end{aligned}
$$

Comparing the two solutions, we must have

$$
F(y)=y,\,G(x)=0.
$$

Therefore, the general solution $u(x,y)=c$ is

$$
2{x}^{3}{y}^{2}+{x}^{4}{y}^{3}+y=c.
$$
